nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish-American; the melodrama and the sensation drama
literary_identity: Playwright and actor; the most successful dramatist of the Victorian stage and the inventor of the sensation drama.
biography: Born Dionysius Lardner Boursiquot in Dublin on 26 December 1820; he made his name with London Assurance (1841), and after emigrating to America in 1853 produced The Poor of New York (1857), The Octoroon (1859), The Colleen Bawn (1860) and The Shaughraun (1874). He died in New York on 18 September 1890.
literary_profile: Dion Boucicault was the most successful dramatist of the Victorian stage and the inventor of the sensation drama: The Colleen Bawn, The Octoroon and The Shaughraun made him the central figure of the popular theatre, and his Irish melodramas created the stage Irishman and the Irish-American theatre.
stylistic_characteristics: The sensation scene of the waterfall or the fire; the Irish peasant dialogue; the comic servant and the villain; the well-made plot of coincidence; the direct, theatrical, crowd-pleasing dramaturgy.
intellectual_concerns: Ireland, Home Rule, and the national question; slavery, emancipation, and the unfinished Reconstruction; empire, jingoism, and the literature of the metropole; the metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital.
historical_significance: Dion Boucicault was the most successful dramatist of the Victorian stage and the inventor of the sensation drama: The Colleen Bawn, The Octoroon and The Shaughraun made him the central figure of the popular theatre.

literary_identity: Actor and theatre manager; the most scholarly producer of Shakespeare of the Victorian stage.
biography: Born Charles John Kean in Waterford on 18 January 1811, the son of the actor Edmund Kean; he made his name at the Haymarket and managed the Princess's Theatre from 1850 to 1859, where his antiquarian productions of Shakespeare set a new standard of historical accuracy. He died in London on 22 January 1868.
literary_profile: Charles Kean was the most scholarly producer of Shakespeare of the Victorian stage: his antiquarian productions at the Princess's Theatre, with their historical research into costume and setting, established the Victorian tradition of the archaeological Shakespeare and made the theatre a vehicle of historical education.
stylistic_characteristics: The antiquarian production with its researched setting; the pictorial staging and the tableau; the historical pageant; the actor-manager's interpretation; the published promptbook and the production record.
intellectual_concerns: Art versus life, and the romance of the artist; the English past and the national history; empire, jingoism, and the literature of the metropole; the metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the American stage and the adaptations
literary_identity: Playwright, critic and theatre manager; the most powerful American theatrical manager of the nineteenth century.
biography: Born John Augustin Daly at Plymouth, North Carolina, on 20 July 1838; he became the drama critic of the New York Daily News and then the manager of the Fifth Avenue Theatre, where he produced his own adaptations — Divorce (1871), Pique (1875), The Big Bonanza (1875) — and the great Shakespeare revivals. He died in Paris on 7 June 1899.
literary_profile: Augustin Daly was the most powerful American theatre manager of the nineteenth century: his adaptations and his company made the American stage a national institution, and his Shakespeare revivals with Ada Rehan set the standard for the American classical theatre.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the critic and the history of English prose
literary_identity: Critic, scholar and historian of literature; the most learned and productive English literary critic of the late nineteenth century.
biography: Born George Edward Bateman Saintsbury in Southampton on 23 October 1845; he taught in Scotland, became a journalist in London, and was Professor of Rhetoric and English Literature at Edinburgh from 1895 to 1915. His History of Nineteenth Century Literature (1896), A Short History of English Literature (1898), A History of English Prose Rhythm (1912) and his edition of the English novelists followed. He died in Bath on 28 January 1933.
literary_profile: George Saintsbury was the most learned and productive English literary critic of the late nineteenth century: his History of Nineteenth Century Literature and his History of English Prose Rhythm made him the central academic critic of the period, and his editions of the English novelists created the canon of English fiction.
stylistic_characteristics: The survey history with its judgements; the technical analysis of prose rhythm; the edition with its introduction; the omnivorous reading and the decisive opinion; the plain, vigorous, confident critical prose.
intellectual_concerns: Art versus life and the romance of the artist; the machinery of print: the serial, the magazine, and the book trade; education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self; the English vernacular and national letters.
historical_significance: George Saintsbury was the most learned and productive English literary critic of the late nineteenth century: his History of Nineteenth Century Literature and his History of English Prose Rhythm made him the central academic critic of the period, and his editions created the canon of English fiction.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the utilitarian ethics and the Cambridge reformer
literary_identity: Philosopher and economist; the author of The Methods of Ethics, the greatest English work of moral philosophy of the century.
biography: Born in Skipton, Yorkshire, on 31 May 1838; he was a fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge, resigned his fellowship in 1869 over the religious tests, and became Knightbridge Professor of Moral Philosophy in 1883. The Methods of Ethics (1874), The Principles of Political Economy (1883) and The Elements of Politics (1891) followed, and he was a founder of Newnham College. He died in Cambridge on 28 August 1900.
literary_profile: Henry Sidgwick wrote The Methods of Ethics, the greatest English work of moral philosophy of the century and the foundation of modern utilitarian ethics: his rigorous analysis of the conflict between self-interest and the general good made him the central moral philosopher of the Victorian age.
stylistic_characteristics: The analytical survey of the competing methods of ethics; the distinction of intuitionism, egoism and utilitarianism; the candid statement of the unresolved problem; the plain, exact, unornamented philosophical prose.
intellectual_concerns: Doubt, agnosticism, and the Broad Church conscience; education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self; science, religion, and the question of design; the woman question, married disability, and the New Woman.
historical_significance: Henry Sidgwick wrote The Methods of Ethics, the greatest English work of moral philosophy of the century and the foundation of modern utilitarian ethics, and he was a founder of Newnham College and of the psychical research that made Cambridge a centre of unorthodox inquiry.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish; the history of morals and the rationalist historian
literary_identity: Historian and philosopher; the author of History of European Morals, the great rationalist history of the Victorian age.
biography: Born William Edward Hartpole Lecky near Dublin on 26 March 1838; he was educated at Trinity College Dublin and made his name with The Leaders of Religious Opinion in Ireland (1861), A History of the Rise and Influence of the Spirit of Rationalism in Europe (1865) and A History of European Morals from Augustus to Charlemagne (1869). He sat as an MP for Dublin University from 1895 and died in London on 22 October 1903.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; the travel narrative, the war despatch and the feminist utopia
literary_identity: Traveller, war correspondent and feminist; the author of Across Patagonia and the suffrage utopia Gloriana.
biography: Born Florence Caroline Douglas at Cummertrees, Dumfriesshire, on 24 May 1855, the daughter of the eighth Marquess of Queensberry and the twin sister of Lord James Douglas; after her father's death in 1858 her mother became a Roman Catholic and took the youngest children to France. She married Sir Alexander Beaumont Churchill Dixie in 1875, published the dramatic tragedy Abel Avenged in 1877, rode across southern Patagonia with her husband, two of her brothers and Julius Beerbohm in 1878-79 and described the journey in Across Patagonia (1880). In 1881 she reported the First Boer War and the aftermath of the Zulu War for the Morning Post and interviewed the captive Cetshwayo, writing In the Land of Misfortune (1882). She published the feminist utopia Gloriana (1890) and two Patagonian books for children, became president of the British Ladies' Football Club in 1895, and died of diphtheria at Glen Stuart, Dumfriesshire, on 7 November 1905.
literary_profile: Lady Florence Dixie was one of the most outspoken aristocratic feminists of the late Victorian press: Across Patagonia presented a woman riding, hunting and enduring on equal terms with the men of her party, her Morning Post despatches from South Africa made her one of the first women war correspondents, and Gloriana imagined a woman who wins the vote for her sex by passing as a man and governing as Prime Minister.
stylistic_characteristics: The first-person narrative of travel, hunting and hardship in a wild landscape; the heroine who equals or outdoes the men around her; the polemical preface and the political fable; the melodramatic plot of disguise, trial and rescue; the direct appeal to the reader on behalf of women.
intellectual_concerns: The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman; education and the professions opened to both sexes; the saddle, the hunting field and the open country; the Zulu kingdom and the war correspondent's conscience; Irish and Scottish Home Rule.
historical_significance: Lady Florence Dixie was one of the most outspoken aristocratic feminists of the late Victorian press: Across Patagonia, her South African despatches and the suffrage utopia Gloriana made her travel, her journalism and her fiction a single argument for the equality of the sexes.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Scottish; Victorian prose, historiography and social criticism
literary_identity: Essayist, historian, translator and social prophet; the great Victorian prose stylist and the moralist against whom the age measured itself.
biography: Born on 4 December 1795, son of a stonemason and Calvinist farmer; educated at Annan Academy and Edinburgh University, where he trained for the ministry and abandoned it. He translated Goethe's Wilhelm Meister (1824) and wrote the Life of Schiller (1825) before his marriage in 1826 to Jane Baillie Welsh, whose letters became one of the great documents of the age. Sartor Resartus appeared in Fraser's Magazine in 1833-34, The French Revolution in 1837, Chartism in 1840, On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History in 1841, Past and Present in 1843, Oliver Cromwell's Letters and Speeches in 1845 and the History of Friedrich II of Prussia in six volumes (1858-65). He gave the lectures that made him famous in 1837-40, refused all honours including the offer of the laureateship, and after Jane's death in 1866 wrote little; he died in Chelsea on 5 February 1881.
literary_profile: Carlyle invented the Victorian prose of prophecy: a style built on capitalised abstractions, apostrophe, Hebraic parallelism, exclamation and a ferocious irony, which he used to indict utilitarianism, laissez-faire political economy, parliamentary talk and the 'cash nexus'. His method in history is to make a document speak — the French Revolution as a 'terrible purification', Cromwell's letters as the voice of a man of God — and his theory of the hero, stated in 1841, was the most influential Victorian account of history as the work of great men. He turned German idealism and Goethe's aesthetics into the common currency of English thought.
stylistic_characteristics: Incarcerated, exclamatory periodic sentences; invented compounds and archaisms; abrupt transitions between the prophetic, the comic and the documentary; direct address to the reader and a self-dramatising narrator; the quotation of primary documents in extenso; the use of symbols (the clothes philosophy, the 'everlasting Yea').
intellectual_concerns: The spiritual condition of the age and the loss of faith; work, the gospel of labour and the dignity of the manual worker; hero-worship and the great man in history; the French Revolution as judgment; the 'cash nexus' and the failure of political economy; silence, sincerity and the contempt of talk; the state and the aristocracy of talent.
historical_significance: Carlyle was the most influential prose writer in Victorian Britain: his French Revolution changed the writing of history, On Heroes supplied the century's theory of leadership, Past and Present its critique of industrialism, and Sartor Resartus its spiritual autobiography. He shaped Ruskin, Arnold, Dickens (to whom he lent the French Revolution while Hard Times was being written), Froude, Kingsley, George Eliot's early criticism and the American Transcendentalists; the twentieth-century reaction against his authoritarianism has not diminished his formal influence on English prose.
